Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM6537 : Advanced Instrumentation in Bioengineering { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Fundamentals of Advanced Instrumentation (Hours 7)
Overview of advanced instrumentation systems in bioengineering, Signal conditioning and data acquisition: Concepts, design, and applications, Principles of bio-electronic interfacing and microcontroller-based systems Real-time data monitoring and processing for biomedical applications.
Module 2: Sensors and Actuators in Bioengineering (Hours 7)
Advanced biosensors: Electrochemical, optical, piezoelectric, and nanobiosensors, Smart sensors for physiological monitoring and wearable devices, Actuator technologies: Piezoelectric, pneumatic, and shape-memory alloy-based systems, Microfluidic and nanofluidic devices in biomedical diagnostics and therapeutics, Integration of sensors and actuators in biomedical devices
Module 3: Advanced Imaging and Diagnostic Instrumentation (Hours 8)
Principles of emerging imaging modalities: Optical coherence tomography (OCT), hyperspectral imaging, and elastography, AI-powered diagnostic tools and handheld imaging devices, Image-guided interventions: Technologies, applications, and innovations, Safety standards, calibration, and regulatory considerations in diagnostic instrumentation
Module 4: Therapeutic Instrumentation and Devices (Hours 7)
Laser-based therapeutic technologies: Photodynamic therapy, laser ablation, and low-level laser therapy, Surgical robotics: Principles, instrumentation, and clinical applications, Bioprinting systems: Instrumentation, techniques, and bio-inks, Advanced instrumentation for targeted drug delivery systems
Module 5: Emerging Trends and Challenges in Bioengineering Instrumentation (Hours 7)
Integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) in biomedical devices, Implantable and portable bio-instrumentation technologies, Miniaturization and nanotechnology in instrumentation Ethical, legal, and regulatory aspects of advanced biomedical devices

Course Objective

1 .

To provide in-depth knowledge of advanced instrumentation technologies used in bioengineering.
2 .

To equip students with skills for designing and applying sensors and actuators in biomedical systems.
3 .

To introduce emerging imaging and therapeutic tools for healthcare applications.
4 .

To explore the challenges and opportunities in modern bioengineering instrumentation.

Course Outcome

1 .

By the end of the course, students will:
1. Understand the principles and applications of advanced instrumentation in bioengineering.
2. Develop and analyze instrumentation systems for biomedical research and healthcare solutions.
3. Address challenges related to miniaturization, safety, and regulation in biomedical devices.
4. Innovate and contribute to the development of next-generation bioengineering instruments and systems
5. Understand the principles and applications of therapeutic tools for healthcare applications.

Essential Reading

1 .

Manz, N. Pamme and D. Iossifidis, Bioanalytical Chemistry, World Scientific Publishing Company

2 .

R. S. Khandour, Handbook of Analytical Instruments, McGraw Hill

Supplementary Reading

1 .

John Enderle, Susan Blanchard, Joseph Bronzino, Introduction to Biomedical Engineering, Academic Press

2 .

H. H. Willard, Instrumental Methods of Analysis, CBS Publishers

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CR3473 : Refractory Laboratory { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Experiment 1:
Determination of packing density of one component system of various particle sizes. 3 Hours

Determination of packing density of two component system using various particle sizes having different weight ratios. 3 Hours
Experiment 3:
Determination of packing density of three component system using various particle sizes having different weight ratios. 6 Hours

Recipe calculation and recipe making for refractory mix using most packed composition. Making of green binder (PVA solution of 4 wt% concentration) 3 Hours

Preparation of refractory brick / shape by dry mixing, mixing with binder, uni-axial pressing, drying and firing. 3 Hours

Characterization of the fired refractory brick / shape by determination of bulk density, apparent porosity and crushing strength. 3 Hours

Determination of shrinkage and PLCR of refractory brick. 3 Hours
Experiment 8:
Processing and casting of castable composition using planetary mixer and vibrator. Curing, drying and firing of the same. 3 Hours

Effect of casting parameter on the properties of castable. 3 Hours

Study of densification and strength development in the castable with temperature. 3 Hours

1. To provide hands-on knowledge of shaped and unshaped refractory manufacturing and characterization techniques

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CS3078 : Time Series Analysis Laboratory { 0-0-2 / 1}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

1. Data Preprocessing: Missing Value Imputation, Normalization, Outlier detection and treatment, Trend, Seasonality and Cyclic component treatment.
2. Time Series Visualization
3. Time Series Forecasting using Statistical Models
4. Time Series Forecasting using Machine Learning Models

9. Fuzzy Time Series Forecasting considering membership values.

Learn techniques for handling missing values, normalization, outlier detection, and treatment in time series data.
2 .

Gain proficiency in visualizing time series data to identify patterns, trends, and seasonality.
3 .

Understand the principles and assumptions underlying classical statistical time series forecasting models.
4 .

Explore the application of machine learning algorithms in crisp and fuzzy time series forecasting.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. Proficient in pre-processing time series.
2. Learn time series visualization techniques.
3. Understand the principles of classical statistical time series forecasting models and be able to apply them to real-world datasets.
4. Understand the crisp and fuzzy time series forecasting employing machine learning models and be able to apply them to real-world datasets.

Subject Nature : Theory

Module 1: Introduction to Fault Tolerant Computing. To understand the fault tolerant design principles

To identify the requirement of fault tolerant systems

To understand fault tolerant distributed systems and its requirement

To design algorithms for fault tolerant systems

Designing and implementing fault tolerant systems for different applications
To identify the policy and mechanisms to achieve fault tolerance

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : PA3413 : Visual Communication { 2-0-0 / 2}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module-I (4 hrs)/ Elements of visual communication: Recognizing the relevance of visual messages and scope for visual communication design introduction to various modes of non-verbal communication (i.e., signs, symbols, imagery, and metaphor) general concepts of visual culture and its relationship with communication design denotative and connotative meanings of visual messages elements of visual communication systems of visual structure or organization of elements (i.e., composition, style, code, etc.) Assignment: Identify elements of communication in a visual message from everyday life and analyze their contribution.
Module-II (8 hrs)/ Theories of visual communication: Introduction to general concepts of communication theory, human perception, and visual ergonomics introduction to reductive logic in graphic design interpretation and visual representation of various ideas, emotions, and human activities Introduction to theories of visual communication: sensory theories (e.g., Gestalt laws, Law of Prägnanz) and perceptual theories (e.g., semiotics, cognitive theory) understanding relationship between syntactic, semantics, and pragmatics of visual language Application of these theories in communication design Assignment: Analyze a visual message for potential application of any communication theory.
Module-III (12 hrs)/ Principles of visual communication: Strategies for gaining attention: contrast, scale, size, proportioning system, colours, ordering principles, sequencing, layering, figure-ground ambivalence, and others Strategies for orienting the user: categorization of information (alphabetically, by time, by location, etc.) visual affordances, navigation, mapping, etc. reading gravity or pattern (e.g., Gutenberg diagram), visual hierarchy and edge relationships elements of typography (typeface, size, font family, alignment, kernelling, combining different fonts, etc.), and others Strategies for interpreting visual messages: reading signs (icon, index, symbol), substitution, appropriation, visual metaphor, etc. Strategies for retaining and extending meaning from visual messages: use of a schema (event, place, or role), use of memory aids (stereotype, archetype, narrative, mnemonics, brand identity, etc.), and others Assignment: Analyze a visual message to identify the strategies adopted to help users interpret the message. Identify the role of the specific cultural context of the target user in easing interpretation.

Course Objective

1 .

To understand the organizational structure of various elements of visual communication design through the application of relevant theories of communication.
2 .

To learn the application of principles of visual communication.
3 .

To sensitize students to the importance of visual communication as an integral part of user experience.

Course Outcome

1 .

1. An ability to recognise the significance of visual aids of communication in user experience design.
2. An ability to apply relevant theories of communication and principles of visual communication in design of visual messages.
3. An ability to understand how visual messages are shaped by the specific context (socio-cultural and physical environments) where it is intended to be used.

Essential Reading

1 .

Davis, M. and Hunt, J., Visual Communication Design: An Introduction to Design Concepts in Everyday Experience, Bloomsbury , 2017

2 .

Smith, K., Handbook of visual communication: theory, methods, and media, Lawrence Erlbaum Associates , 2005

Supplementary Reading

1 .

Baldwin, J., Lucienne. R., Visual Communication, from theory to practice, AVA Publishing SA , 2006

2 .

Williams, R., Newton, J., Visual Communication: Integrating Media, Art, and Science, Routledge , 2007

6005.t: HS5424: Poverty, Inequality and Human Development
6005.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : HS5424 : Poverty, Inequality and Human Development { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Unit 1: Conceptual dimensions of poverty welfarist (utility , income) and non-welfarist (basic needs, human development and capability) approaches deprivation and human development absolute and relative poverty measures notions of chronic poverty and socio-economic vulnerability with particular emphasis given to the role of health functioning and capability deprivation
Unit 2: Inequity vs. Inequality Inequality measurement: Lorenz curve, Gini index, concentration index Economic inequalities in India measuring international and global inequality: unweighted international inequality, population-weighted international inequality, true world income distribution Basic problem in inequality measurement
Unit 3: The economic growth, poverty and inequality triangle the inverted U hypothesis income and inequality: uneven and compensatory changes Inequality, saving, income and growth Inequality and Growth: Evidence Inequality and demand composition Inequality, capital market and development, decomposition of socio-economic inequality
Unit 4: Measurement of Human Development Index (HDI), Gender-related Development Index (GDI), Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM), Human Poverty Index (HPI) , Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI).

Course Objective

1 .

This course aims at equipping students with the technical and substantive dimensions of various measures of poverty, inequality and human development.

Course Outcome

1 .

On successful completion of the course, students will be able to:
1. Describe the theoretical and technical aspects of poverty measurement at the global and national level.
2. Understand equity and inequality and its linkage with the process of development.
3. Examine the linkage between economic growth, poverty and inequality.
4. Understand and estimate various composite development indicators like HDI, GDI, and MPI.

Essential Reading

Debraj Ray, Development Economics, , Oxford University Press, 2009

Sen, A. K., On Economic Inequality, Oxford University Press, Oxford

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : FP4208 : Experimental Design and Statistical Methods { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1: Basic statistical concepts, concepts
Module 2: Descriptive statistics, Mean, Variance,
Module 3: Data and its nature, data representation, diagrams and graphs using MS Excel,
Module 4: Measure of central tendency, Dispersion, Swekness and Kurtosis.
Module 5: Probability, Probability distribution.
Module 6: Introduction to the theory of estimation and confidence-intervals
Module 7: Analysis of variance.

Course Objective

1 .

To learn about various basic and advanced concepts of statistics.

To learn methods of experimental design, basic to advanced

To be able to articulate, case based analyses and apply the appropriate method of analyses.

1. To be able to understand the data distribution and pattern.
2. To be able to conduct descriptive analyses.
3. To be able to conduct ANOVA analyses based on the provided data set.
4. To decide factors and responses for a controlled experiment and prepare an experimental design.
5. To carry out a regression analysis for any data.
